title: The Scientific Method in Biology
summary: Scientists use a step‑by‑step process to turn curiosity into reliable knowledge. This lesson shows how observation, hypothesis, experiment, and analysis work together in biology.

sections.heading: Observation
sections.body:
Observation is the first step. A biologist might notice that a pond has many algae when the water is warm. This careful watching raises a question about why the algae grow faster in warm water.

Observations can be simple (seeing a plant wilt) or use tools (microscopes, sensors). They give the raw data that spark scientific questions.

sections.heading: Hypothesis
sections.body:
A hypothesis is an educated guess that explains the observation. For the pond example, a hypothesis could be: "Algae grow faster when water temperature is above 25°C because warmer water speeds up photosynthesis."

A good hypothesis is testable and specific, so it can be proved right or wrong by an experiment.

sections.heading: Experiment
sections.body:
An experiment is a controlled test of the hypothesis. The biologist could set up three identical tanks at 20°C, 25°C, and 30°C, adding the same amount of algae and light. All other factors stay the same.

The experiment must include a control (the condition you compare against) and repeat trials to ensure reliable results.

sections.heading: Analysis
sections.body:
After the experiment, the scientist records how much algae grew in each tank. Analysis means comparing the data, often with simple graphs or calculations. If the 30°C tank shows the most growth, the hypothesis is supported.

If the data don’t match the prediction, the scientist revises the hypothesis or looks for other variables, showing how science is an ongoing cycle.

key_terms.meaning: Careful noticing of natural phenomena, often using senses or tools.
A testable explanation for an observation.
A controlled procedure to test a hypothesis.
The standard condition in an experiment used for comparison.
Examining data to see if it supports or refutes the hypothesis.
Any factor that can change in an experiment; includes independent and dependent variables.

quiz.q: What is the first step of the scientific method?
quiz.why: Science starts with observing a phenomenon before forming a hypothesis.

quiz.q: In an experiment, the variable that the scientist changes is the:
quiz.why: The independent variable is deliberately altered to test its effect.

quiz.q: If the data do not support the hypothesis, the scientist should:
options: Revise the hypothesis or design a new experiment
quiz.why: Science is iterative; unexpected results lead to new hypotheses or experiments.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a control group?
options: To provide a baseline for comparison
quiz.why: A control shows what happens without the experimental treatment.

flashcards.back: The act of noticing and recording facts about the natural world.
A testable statement that explains an observation.
The factor that is intentionally changed in an experiment.
A group that does not receive the experimental treatment, used for comparison.
The process of interpreting data to determine if the hypothesis is supported.
